title: Crystal Ball ORB
method: Subjective author probabilities, not calibrated model outputs or market odds. This edition contains technology, culture, sport, spaceflight, prices and weather forecasts. Calendar facts, rumors and guesses are distinguished in each reading. There is no automatic outcome monitoring. Five retained calls preserve their earlier cutoffs; five replacements have this edition’s cutoff. Correlated and selected calls do not establish AGI or foreknowledge.

points.label: Everyday prices
points.title: A number that reaches the household
points.body: A price release offers one small window into everyday costs. This branch follows a defined measurement from a previous reading to a new result. A national index is not your personal shopping basket, and one monthly movement is not a complete economic story.

points.label: Everyday sci-fi
points.title: When tomorrow fits in your pocket
points.body: A screen that unfolds and a helper that can act for you make the future tangible. Follow the difference between an introduction and a product you can use, or between a promise of autonomy and the permissions that govern it.

edge.backward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: The spotlight
points.title: The envelope can still surprise you
points.body: Awards make professional recognition visible, but nomination totals do not reveal a final ballot. The two Emmy calls share an evidence source and a ceremony; treat that dependence as a limit on what their results can teach.

points.label: Competitive depth
points.title: What carries through to the final?
points.body: Past strength is useful context for sport, while opponents, event order and fatigue keep the outcome open. One branch follows an early medal table; another follows the shape of a final without choosing its winner.

points.label: Orbital lifelines
points.title: The most important spacecraft may carry groceries
points.body: Food, fuel, spare parts and crew rotations sustain work in orbit. A launch schedule is a plan with dependencies, not a completed journey. Our small UAP wink belongs here as playful design; these branches concern identified spacecraft and documented milestones.

points.label: Changing skies
points.title: A quiet forecast still needs watching
points.body: A short-term outlook can support a modest expectation without guaranteeing safety. Formation, intensity and local impacts are separate questions. This branch follows one observable basin-wide event while keeping real-world warnings above our experiment.

points.label: Core CPI 0.2–0.3%
points.title: US core CPI rises 0.2% or 0.3% in August
points.body: My guess is a seasonally adjusted monthly core CPI increase reported as 0.2% or 0.3%. July’s 0.2% reading gives a modest starting point, while an energy shock leaves room for indirect pressure. This is a simple persistence judgment, not an econometric nowcast. Core CPI excludes food and energy directly; it is not the Fed’s preferred PCE measure.
points.test: YES if the initial September 11 BLS release reports August CPI-U, all items less food and energy, at 0.2% or 0.3% month over month, seasonally adjusted. Use the published rounded figure, not later revisions.
points.alternative: A softer 0.0–0.1% reading, or an upside surprise of 0.4% or more.
points.watch: The core monthly line in the initial release and the shelter and goods components.

points.label: July core +0.2%
points.title: The previous monthly core reading
points.body: The July release reported core CPI up 0.2% month over month, seasonally adjusted. A single month is a weak trend estimate. I use it as an anchor for the next report, with a wider 0.2–0.3% success range rather than pretending to know the next decimal.
points.question: How stable is the July pace across major components?
points.method: Inspect the archived release and compare the next release’s component contributions.

points.label: Component surprise?
points.title: Knowledge floor · Where could the surprise hide?
points.body: This edition does not contain a bottom-up rent, vehicle, airfare, and medical-price nowcast. That missing work limits the confidence of the numerical call. Energy pressures can transmit into core categories indirectly and with lags.
points.question: Which component could move the rounded core rate outside the forecast range?
points.method: Build a contribution table from official category weights and monthly movements after release; retain the original forecast.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: China leads
points.title: China leads the Asian Games gold table by September 22
points.event: Asian Games open September 19 · early medal race
points.body: I expect China to lead the gold-medal table after competition on September 22 in Japan. Its long record makes it the strongest starting choice, but opening-week event order and Japan’s home advantage can disrupt the early table. This prediction deliberately stops inside the two-week window: it does not pretend the October 4 closing results are already in scope.
points.test: YES if China is ranked first by gold medals on the official table at September 22, 23:59 Japan time. Break ties by silver then bronze; an exact tie counts as joint first and YES. If no medals have been awarded or no official tally is recoverable, leave unresolved.
points.alternative: Japan or another delegation leads the early table because the first medal events favor its strengths.
points.watch: The actual medal schedule and official daily gold, silver, and bronze totals.

points.label: Eleven straight
points.title: Historical depth across many sports
points.body: The Olympic Council of Asia reports that China topped the medal table at eleven consecutive Asian Games through Hangzhou, where it won 201 golds. That supports a strong tournament-level prior. It is weaker evidence for the first few days of a different Games.
points.question: How well does a full-Games record transfer to an early table?
points.method: Map the first medal events to recent international results before increasing confidence.

points.label: Early-event bias
points.title: Knowledge floor · The order of finals matters
points.body: This edition does not include an event-by-event medal simulation. A different early programme could make a normally dominant team trail temporarily. That is the principal uncertainty in moving from historical dominance to a September 22 snapshot.
points.question: Which delegation benefits most from the first medal days?
points.method: Add the official daily final schedule and likely entrants; keep hypothetical medals distinct from completed results.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: The iPhone folds
points.title: Apple introduces a folding iPhone
points.body: Picture the familiar rectangle opening like a small book. My call is that Apple formally introduces an iPhone with a folding display at its September 9 event. The event is confirmed; the product remains a rumor at this cutoff. I give the repeated preview reporting substantial weight, while allowing for a delayed reveal. Seventy-five percent is an author judgment, not inside information or a market price.
points.test: YES if Apple officially presents an Apple-branded iPhone with a display that physically folds during the September 9 event or in its associated same-day newsroom announcement, by 23:59 America/Los_Angeles. A patent, analyst rumor, hinged accessory or two rigid screens does not qualify. An announcement counts even if shipping is later. If the event occurs without this introduction, NO; cancellation beyond the window is unresolved.
points.alternative: Apple keeps the new design offstage, or reveals a different product while the folding iPhone stays in rumor territory.
points.watch: The official event recording and product newsroom page; identify the actual flexible display and separate reveal, preorder and delivery dates.
points.stakes: A reveal could push developers and rival manufacturers toward different screen layouts. For buyers, the meaningful next questions would be price, durability and repairability. An announcement alone cannot answer them.
points.concern: A convincing demo is not evidence of long-term hinge durability or an affordable device. Treat launch excitement and product reliability as different claims.

edge.backward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: Stage vs rumor
points.title: A confirmed stage, an unconfirmed device
points.body: Apple invites viewers to a September 9 event. A September 7 Tom’s Guide preview expects a folding iPhone. The invitation supports the date; the preview supplies the speculative product lead. Neither is a completed launch result.
points.question: How much independent evidence sits behind the repeated rumors?
points.method: Trace original reporting where possible. Repeated articles can share one upstream source and should not be counted as independent confirmations.

edge.backward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: Reveal ≠ release
points.title: Knowledge floor · The future may arrive in stages
points.body: This call deliberately tests an introduction. It makes no claim about stock on shelves, sales volume, quality or whether a folding phone is useful to you. Those deserve separate tests after specifications and independent reviews exist.
points.question: What would make this more than an impressive stage prop?
points.method: Record shipping dates and specifications, then seek independent durability and usability evidence. Keep those later assessments separate from this frozen reveal prediction.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.
edge.backward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: The Pitt wins
points.title: The Pitt wins Outstanding Drama Series
points.body: The envelope opens; my pick is The Pitt. The Television Academy lists it among the drama nominees and reports 25 nominations across categories. That breadth suggests professional enthusiasm, but it is not a count of final-round votes. I give it a modest edge over the field. The fun is a real possibility of being surprised, not a promise that the favorite must win.
points.test: YES if the Television Academy names The Pitt the winner or an official co-winner of Outstanding Drama Series at the September 14, 2026 ceremony. Any other sole winner is NO. Use the Academy’s category result, not acting or Creative Arts awards. If the category is not awarded by September 22, leave unresolved.
points.alternative: Another nominated drama converts its own passionate voting bloc into the top award.
points.watch: The Academy’s Outstanding Drama Series result after the ceremony. Earlier Creative Arts wins do not resolve this category.
points.stakes: The winner may gain new viewers and become a useful signal for commissioning and promotion. Those effects are possibilities; this call scores only the award, not a ratings increase.
points.concern: Awards measure the choices of an eligible voting body. They do not establish an objective best show or imply that fictional medical scenes are clinical guidance.

points.label: 25 nominations
points.title: Breadth of recognition is a clue
points.body: The Academy reports 25 nominations for The Pitt and places the main ceremony on Monday, September 14. Its show page lists Outstanding Drama Series. Nomination totals span different categories, so they cannot be converted directly into winner probabilities.
points.question: Does broad recognition predict this particular final vote?
points.method: Compare category-specific past nomination and win records before fitting a numerical model; no such model was used for this 60% estimate.

points.label: Secret ballots
points.title: Knowledge floor · Enthusiasm is not a vote tally
points.body: The missing information is the final distribution of votes. Public acclaim, campaign visibility and nomination totals are indirect signals. This orb has no access to ballots and no verified betting consensus.
points.question: Could a smaller but more concentrated coalition beat the apparent favorite?
points.method: Write down the strongest rival case before the ceremony. Preserve the 60% estimate even if later coverage changes the mood.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: AI still asks
points.title: Muse still requires approval before purchases
points.body: Here is the everyday science-fiction question: will your digital helper still stop at the checkout? My call is that Meta’s published Muse design continues to require user approval before making a purchase at the end of this window. The launch description explicitly includes that checkpoint. I expect the permission boundary to outlast the first wave of excitement about autonomy.
points.test: YES if Meta’s current official Muse documentation at September 22, 23:59 UTC explicitly retains a requirement for user approval before making purchases. NO if current official documentation explicitly permits purchases without such approval, including a newly introduced autonomous-spending mode. If the current rule is absent, ambiguous or inaccessible, leave unresolved. A launch article alone is insufficient if newer documentation supersedes it. This tests the published permission policy, not whether every real execution obeys it.
points.alternative: Meta introduces a documented mode allowing purchases without individual approval, or changes the checkpoint as the product evolves.
points.watch: Current official permission and purchase documentation, with dated copies and change history. Separate a policy change from an alleged bug or a fabricated screenshot.
points.stakes: The boundary matters whenever AI moves from suggesting an action to committing a person’s money. More autonomy could reduce effort while increasing the cost of misunderstandings. Approval design is a practical question even without agreeing on the word AGI.
points.concern: A vendor’s safety description is not an independent security audit. This forecast does not assert that Muse is AGI, always reliable, or immune to malicious instructions and mistaken purchases.

points.label: The checkout pause
points.title: An explicit approval checkpoint at launch
points.body: Meta’s September 8 introduction says Muse seeks approval before sending an email or making a purchase. It also describes work continuing after the app closes. These are the vendor’s stated design and capability claims, not independent evidence of flawless execution.
points.question: Does later official documentation preserve the same purchase boundary?
points.method: Save the launch wording and compare it with current permission documentation at the deadline. Resolve the policy test separately from real-world reliability reports.

points.label: Policy vs behavior
points.title: Knowledge floor · Stated safeguards need testing
points.body: The missing evidence is independent observation across ordinary and adversarial use. A documented approval requirement can coexist with implementation failures. Conversely, a user-approved action is not evidence of unauthorized autonomy.
points.question: How often does the system ask at the right moment, with enough information to decide?
points.method: Use authorized, controlled tests with harmless transactions and clear records. Never expose someone else’s accounts or spend money merely to score this orb.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: Cargo reaches orbit
points.title: Progress 96 docks with the ISS by September 22
points.event: Progress 96 docks with the ISS by September 22
points.body: A quiet spacecraft arrives with the things that keep an orbital laboratory running. My narrow lean is that Progress 96 docks with the International Space Station before our window closes. NASA’s earlier plan named a September 9 launch and September 11 docking, but its current event page says the timing is under review. That change is the main reason for only 60% confidence.
points.test: YES if NASA or the spacecraft operator confirms completed docking of Progress 96 to the ISS after this cutoff and by September 22, 23:59 UTC. Liftoff, orbit insertion, an approach or a rescheduled appointment is insufficient. NO if reliable mission reporting establishes no docking by then, including delay or failure; unresolved if status cannot be established.
points.alternative: Schedule review leads to a later launch or docking, or an operational problem interrupts the journey.
points.watch: The revised official timetable, then the actual docking confirmation and timestamp. The old September 11 target is not a confirmed appointment.
points.stakes: A completed delivery would replenish supplies supporting people and experiments aboard the station. The practical milestone is arrival, not the spectacle of liftoff.
points.concern: A delay alone does not establish an emergency aboard the station. Inventory, backup plans and crew safety cannot be inferred from this calendar call.

points.label: Plan under review
points.title: The schedule changed underneath the story
points.body: NASA describes a cargo load of about three tons. Its release retained an earlier launch-and-docking plan while noting that coverage details await an update. The dedicated event page now marks the date under review. That direct status qualifies the earlier dates.
points.question: What timetable replaces the earlier plan?
points.method: Prefer the current event notice, then the actual mission report. Record both the publication time and the event time.

points.label: Docking is the test
points.title: Knowledge floor · Arrival has several gates
points.body: Launch, rendezvous and docking are distinct steps. This edition has no engineering reliability model or inside view of readiness, so the probability is an author judgment about completing the chain.
points.question: Which gate accounts for the most remaining uncertainty?
points.method: Use documented readiness updates. Do not invent a cause for the schedule review or infer success from a launch video.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.

points.label: Crew launch waits
points.title: Crew-13 has not launched by September 22
points.event: Crew-13 has not launched by September 22
points.body: The crystal ball’s quieter prediction is sometimes that the countdown waits. NASA lists Crew-13 as no earlier than late September. I expect the mission still to be on the ground at our September 22 deadline. The phrase is broad enough that I leave a real chance of a launch within the final days of this window; it does not mean a fixed date after the 22nd.
points.test: YES if Crew-13 has not lifted off by September 22, 23:59 UTC. NO if an actual Crew-13 liftoff occurs after this cutoff and before that deadline, even if the flight later aborts. A rehearsal, static-fire test or new target date is not liftoff. Use official NASA/SpaceX mission reporting; leave unresolved if a reliable status cannot be established.
points.alternative: Readiness and scheduling align for a launch on or before September 22.
points.watch: A specific launch target, readiness notices and actual liftoff reporting; distinguish a launch attempt from a launch.
points.stakes: Crew rotations shape station operations and research planning. A later launch may shift those plans without changing the mission’s long-term purpose.
points.concern: A timetable is not a diagnosis of a hardware problem. Do not infer crew danger or failure from a mission remaining on the ground.

edge.forward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: No earlier than
points.title: A lower bound, not a reservation
points.body: NASA’s event page says no earlier than late September and describes a long-duration science expedition to the ISS. The source supplies the schedule boundary; the choice of 80% is this author’s judgment.
points.question: Does a specific target date materially change the expectation?
points.method: Keep the original probability and write any revised estimate as a new dated entry.

edge.forward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: Calendar ≠ readiness
points.title: Knowledge floor · What the public schedule omits
points.body: The page does not provide a complete readiness model. Vehicle, station and launch-range planning can all matter, but this orb has not measured their individual contribution.
points.question: Which dependency is actually documented as controlling the date?
points.method: Attribute any delay explanation to a named mission source. Avoid filling a public information gap with a technical-sounding story.

edge.down: Evidence boundary: follow the open question to develop this branch.
edge.forward: Edge of this dated forecast thread.

points.label: Hacks takes comedy
points.title: Hacks wins Outstanding Comedy Series
points.body: My comedy-night pick is Hacks. The Television Academy reports 24 nominations across categories, a strong sign of recognition. I give it a modest edge for Outstanding Comedy Series while allowing a substantial chance that another nominee takes the envelope. This is a subjective pick, not a forecast derived from private ballots.
points.test: YES if the Television Academy names Hacks the winner or official co-winner of Outstanding Comedy Series at the September 14, 2026 ceremony. A different sole winner is NO. Acting, writing and earlier Creative Arts results do not count. If the category is not awarded by September 22, leave unresolved.
points.alternative: A rival comedy wins the final vote despite Hacks’ broad nomination showing.
points.watch: The Academy’s category-specific winner record after the main ceremony.
points.stakes: A win could send new viewers toward the series and affect its place in the cultural conversation. Those possible effects are not additional scored claims.
points.concern: Awards reflect a voting body’s choices. Nomination totals across categories cannot be treated as votes for the top series award.

points.label: 24 nominations
points.title: Recognition spread across the production
points.body: The Academy’s nomination announcement reports 24 nominations for Hacks and a September 14 main ceremony. The show’s official awards page lists its categories. This provides a real basis for a favorite, but not a mathematical conversion to 60%.
points.question: How much does broad recognition transfer to the series ballot?
points.method: Compare category-specific historical results before fitting a model; no such model is claimed here.

points.label: The rival case
points.title: Knowledge floor · Who has the concentrated support?
points.body: The missing evidence is final vote distribution. A series with fewer nominations can still have enough concentrated support to win the main category.
points.question: What is the strongest argument for another nominee?
points.method: Write that argument before the envelope opens. Do not revise the original pick after seeing results.

points.label: A fourth set
points.title: The US Open men’s final lasts at least four completed sets
points.event: The US Open men’s final lasts at least four completed sets
points.body: Give the final one more act. My slight lean is that both finalists win a set and the match finishes in four or five sets. The men’s singles format allows that, and the previous final lasted four sets, but one example is weak evidence. At 55%, this is intentionally a close, entertaining call about match shape rather than a confident model of the finalists.
points.test: YES if the 2026 US Open men’s singles final ends with four or five fully completed sets in the official score. A completed three-set final is NO. Retirement, walkover, disqualification or an unfinished match is unresolved regardless of partial-set count. If postponed, use a completed final by September 22; otherwise unresolved.
points.alternative: One finalist controls the match and wins in three completed sets.
points.watch: The official final score and any retirement or interruption notation, not the number of hours on court.
points.stakes: A longer final would give spectators more swings of momentum and put another layer of endurance on display. Match length alone says little about its quality.
points.concern: This is for observation and learning. It is not betting advice, and a long match is not evidence that an athlete is healthy or injured.

points.label: Best of five
points.title: The format creates room for a comeback
points.body: USTA’s guide specifies best-of-five sets for men’s singles. ATP schedules the final for September 13 and records a four-set final in 2025. Those facts explain the test; they do not establish how often it should succeed.
points.question: What would a longer historical sample say about four-or-five-set finals?
points.method: Count completed finals using a consistent retirement rule, then compare that base rate with this subjective 55%.

points.label: Matchup unknowns
points.title: Knowledge floor · A format is not a probability model
points.body: This edition does not use a point-by-point simulation, live odds or a medical assessment. Serve strength, return strength and fatigue could matter, but their effects have not been estimated here.
points.question: Would a matchup model materially move the probability away from 55%?
points.method: Build it using information available before the final. Score the frozen prediction separately from any later model.

points.label: A quieter Atlantic
points.title: No new Atlantic tropical cyclone through September 14 noon UTC
points.event: No new Atlantic tropical cyclone through September 14 noon UTC
points.body: A welcome possibility is a few quieter days. I lean toward no newly designated Atlantic tropical or subtropical cyclone between this cutoff and September 14 at noon UTC. The retrieved NHC outlook issued September 7 at 08:00 EDT expects no formation over seven days. That source is already dated, so I stop at the end of its stated horizon and keep confidence modest rather than extending it through the whole fortnight.
points.test: YES if NHC operational advisories identify no newly formed tropical or subtropical depression or storm in the Atlantic basin after this cutoff through September 14, 12:00 UTC. A new depression counts and makes the forecast NO even if it is never named. A potential tropical cyclone designation alone does not count. Use advisory issue times; if the advisory archive cannot be checked completely, unresolved. Later best-track reanalysis does not change this operational-reporting test.
points.alternative: A new disturbance organizes quickly enough for NHC to designate a tropical or subtropical cyclone within this short interval.
points.watch: New official outlooks and the complete NHC advisory archive. Live safety decisions must use current official warnings, not this saved forecast.
points.stakes: A period without new formation could reduce one source of disruption. It would not rule out damaging rain, coastal hazards, existing systems or risks in other ocean basins.
points.concern: No new cyclone does not mean safe weather. This is a dated educational snapshot with no automatic updates; follow local authorities and current NHC guidance for real decisions.

points.label: A dated outlook
points.title: The retrieved text has its own clock
points.body: The Atlantic section of the retrieved NHC page is dated September 7, 08:00 EDT and states that formation is not expected in the next seven days. Other sections describe other basins. This branch uses only the Atlantic text and discloses its age.
points.question: Has newer official guidance identified a disturbance?
points.method: Compare issue times and basin labels. Preserve this original call even when a subsequent outlook changes.

points.label: Quiet ≠ safe
points.title: Knowledge floor · Formation is only one hazard
points.body: This test counts new cyclone designations, not rainfall, local flooding, wind at a particular address or total seasonal activity. This orb has no local hazard model.
points.question: Which important risks remain even if the formation call is right?
points.method: Consult location-specific official warnings. Do not generalize a basin-wide absence of new cyclones into a personal safety forecast.
